items.text: States that a confident, well-written text (from an AI or a person) is not evidence that its claims are true.
items.feedback_fail: Start with the core point: smooth, confident writing is not evidence that the claims are true.

items.text: Recommends leaving the page to check a claim: looking for an independent, trustworthy source instead of reading the same page harder.
items.feedback_fail: Add the key move: leave the page and look for an independent, trustworthy source that confirms or denies the claim.

items.text: Names at least one concrete check: who is behind the source, whether other outlets report it, or whether a date/number can be verified.
items.feedback_fail: Name one concrete check: who is behind the source, whether others report the same, or whether a date or number can be verified.

items.text: Draws a practical consequence: before forwarding or relying on a surprising claim, verify it first.
items.feedback_fail: Close with the habit: before you forward or rely on a surprising claim, verify it first.

misconception_strings: if it is well written it is true
you can trust the source if it looks professional

anchors.pass_example: A smooth, confident text proves nothing — an AI or a person can write nonsense beautifully. So I don't read the same page harder; I leave it and check what independent, trustworthy sources say about the claim. I look at who is behind it and whether anyone else reliable reports the same fact or date. Before I forward anything surprising, I verify it first.
anchors.fail_example: You can usually tell misinformation by bad spelling and unprofessional design, so a well-written AI answer from a polished site is safe to trust and share.
